title: Working Agreements
description: Working agreements that the team will actually follow — versus the wall of post-its that gets ignored after one sprint. Three to five agreements, each one a specific behaviour, each one the result of a real conversation. The discipline is in the revision: a working agreement that hasn't been revised in a quarter has stopped being a working agreement.

# Customer Portal Team — Working Agreements
_Established 12 April 2026 (week 6 retro) · last revised 16 May 2026 (week 11 retro)_

## How we wrote these

In the week 6 retro, the team surfaced two recurring frictions: code-review wait times (Lewis was bottlenecking everything; PRs sitting 2-3 days), and a creeping pattern of standup running 25-30 minutes with deep technical conversations. The team agreed three things in the room; we added a fourth in the week 8 retro after the customer-event rollback.

## Our agreements

### 1. Code review SLA — 24 hours, first response.
- **What:** Every open PR gets a first response from a reviewer within 24 hours. 'First response' can be 'I'll look at this tomorrow morning' — it's about acknowledgement, not full review.
- **Why:** PRs were sitting 2-3 days; engineers were context-switching back to old work. The 24-hour first-response cut median age of an open PR from 38 hours to 14 hours within two sprints.
- **Revisit if:** team capacity changes (someone leaves, two people on leave at once) or median creeps back above 24 hours for two sprints.

### 2. Standup is 15 minutes. No problem-solving in the room.
- **What:** Round the board, blockers noted, deep conversations moved to a sidebar booked by the SM during standup itself.
- **Why:** Standup had been drifting to 25-30 min with technical deep-dives. Half the room was checking out; the SM was absorbing the time cost.
- **Revisit if:** the team feels they're not getting enough collaborative time. Note: refinement and ad-hoc working sessions are where collaborative time should be, not standup.

### 3. No production deploys after Thursday 4pm.
- **What:** No production deploys after 4pm Thursday. Friday morning is OK if explicitly agreed at standup.
- **Why:** The week-8 rollback shipped Friday 5pm; nobody was around Saturday to monitor. Lewis had committed to himself privately not to do this; making it a team agreement made it everyone's responsibility, not just his.
- **Revisit if:** the team has a production-ready feature that's been waiting >2 days. Some Friday-afternoon deploys may be net-positive; the agreement is a default, not a rule.

### 4. The QA tail of any payments-touching story is owned by Naledi, sized by Naledi, signed off by Naledi.
- **What:** For any story that touches the payments pipeline, Naledi owns the QA scope. Dev sizing without QA sizing = an incomplete estimate.
- **Why:** Surfaced in week 8 retro (the rollback). Naledi had been carrying the QA tail invisibly; the team agreement makes it visible.
- **Revisit if:** Naledi changes roles or the payments-pipeline scope changes materially.

## What we tried and dropped

### A pair-programming rotation (week 4–week 6)

We tried a Monday-morning pair-programming session as a working agreement. Dropped at the week 6 retro because: the team is already pair-programming organically on hard problems; the formal Monday slot was redundant; people resented the calendar block. The lesson: working agreements should formalise what's working, not impose what isn't.

annotations.note: How-we-wrote-these is the provenance. Teams forget within six weeks why an agreement exists; the provenance is the answer. Without it, agreements get cut for the wrong reasons (a new team member finds them annoying and the rationale is lost).
Three to five. Not ten. A list of fifteen working agreements is a fiction — nobody can remember them, nobody follows them. The discipline is picking the ones that actually matter.

Each agreement has a 'revisit if' trigger. Without it, the agreement becomes permanent regardless of whether it's still useful. The trigger forces the team to actually re-evaluate, instead of waiting for someone to bring it up.

'What we tried and dropped' is the section most teams skip. It's also the section that teaches new team members the most. Reading 'we tried a pair-programming rotation and cut it' tells a new joiner more about how this team works than any introduction document.

common_mistakes: Working agreements written by the SM and presented to the team. Wrong. The team writes them; the SM facilitates the writing.
Too many agreements. A wall of fifteen post-its is the kind of working-agreements list that gets ignored. Three to five is the band where the team can actually remember them.
Agreements without a 'revisit if' trigger. They become permanent regardless of whether they're still useful. New team members inherit them without knowing why; old patterns ossify.
Agreements about values rather than behaviours. 'We respect each other' is not a working agreement; it's a slogan. 'We don't ship past Thursday 4pm without an explicit decision' is an agreement.

Agreements never revisited. The team adopted them in week 6, the SM filed them in a drive folder, nobody reads them again. Set a recurring 6-week revisit; first time you do it, the team will discover an agreement that's silently stopped being followed.
What-we-tried-and-dropped omitted. Loses the institutional memory of why certain things were attempted. Teams cycle through the same failed experiments.
variant_patterns: New team variant: don't write working agreements until week 4-5. Before that, the team doesn't know enough about itself to write useful ones. Forcing it earlier produces theatre.
Team-merge variant (two teams becoming one): existing agreements from both teams get surfaced, discussed, and either kept, merged, or dropped. The conversation itself is the most valuable part.

Cross-functional team variant (including stakeholders outside engineering): agreements may need to cover interaction patterns with adjacent functions (CS, finance, ops). Keep these separate from internal team agreements — different audiences, different cadences.
